name: The Ebon Well

detectability.signature: Concentrated gravitational field consistent with a planetary-mass object, but with no corresponding mass detectable at the source; gravimetric sensors register a smooth gradient intensifying toward the center

proximity: Navigation sensors register a massive gravitational body directly ahead that does not appear on visual or radar scans
Orbital trajectories bend toward the well's center, requiring corrective thrust to maintain course
Nearby debris and dust slowly spiral inward, forming a faint accretion pattern around nothing visible
contact: Ships experience gravitational pull equivalent to a small terrestrial planet, approximately 0.4g at the center
Uncontrolled descent toward the well's center accelerates gradually, requiring significant thrust to escape
Sensor systems overload attempting to reconcile gravitational readings with the absence of any physical mass
prolonged_exposure: Vessels in stable orbit around the well experience cumulative navigational drift as instruments attempt to model a mass that does not exist
Structural fatigue from sustained tidal stress in a gradient that behaves like a planet's but emanates from empty space
Crew report a persistent psychological weight — a heaviness of spirit that mirrors the anomalous gravity

phenomena: A thin disk of accreted dust and micrometeorites orbits the well's invisible center, giving it the appearance of a planet-sized ring system surrounding nothing
Light passing near the center bends measurably, producing gravitational lensing effects consistent with a body of approximately 0.3 Earth masses
Objects dropped toward the center decelerate as expected for a gravity well but never impact a surface — they simply oscillate back and forth through the center like pendulums in empty space
hazards: Unsuspecting vessels may be drawn into an unplanned orbit or descent toward the invisible center
The absence of a visible mass source makes the well difficult to identify without gravimetric instruments
Escape velocity at the center requires sustained thrust, potentially straining fuel reserves of smaller craft
opportunities: The well provides a free gravitational anchor for orbital installations without the complications of a physical planetary body
Study of the phantom mass could illuminate dark matter interactions or unknown gravitational phenomena
The accreted debris disk contains concentrated minerals drawn from a wide surrounding volume of space
known_incidents: The prospector ship Cairn Moth was the first to encounter the Ebon Well in 2302, when its pilot noticed fuel consumption increasing without any visible cause; investigation revealed the ship had entered a stable orbit around what appeared to be empty space

In 2378, the University of Aldren constructed a small research station in stable orbit around the well's center, making it the only inhabited installation in known space that orbits an invisible, massless gravitational source
description: The Ebon Well is a gravitational anomaly of profound simplicity and profound mystery: a gravity well with no mass at its center. It exerts a gravitational pull consistent with a small terrestrial body of approximately 0.3 Earth masses, complete with a smooth gradient, tidal effects, and orbital mechanics. Yet at its heart there is nothing — no planet, no dense matter, no collapsed star. Only empty space, pulling everything toward it with patient, invisible hands. A faint disk of accumulated dust and debris orbits the center, giving the well its only visual signature: a ghostly ring system encircling absolute emptiness.

Ships entering the well's influence experience the familiar tug of gravity and must adjust their trajectories accordingly. The effect is moderate — strong enough to capture unwary vessels into orbit but manageable with standard thrust. The true disorientation comes from the instruments: gravimetric sensors insist a planetary body exists at the center, while every other detector reports vacuum. Objects released at the center do not rest — they oscillate through the focal point in long, slow arcs, behaving as though falling through a planet that isn't there.

The Ebon Well has been studied extensively since its discovery early in the 24th century, and it has resisted every attempt at explanation. It is not a black hole — there is no event horizon, no relativistic effects. It is not dark matter in any conventional model — the concentration is too precise, too structured. Some theorists propose it as a topological knot in spacetime that mimics mass without containing it; others suggest it is the gravitational shadow of a massive object in an adjacent dimension. None of these theories have been proven.

Today, the Ebon Well serves as both a research site and a navigational curiosity. The University of Aldren's orbital station continues its long-term study, and the accreted debris disk has become a minor resource harvesting site for minerals concentrated from the surrounding volume of space. For travelers, the well is a gentle reminder that gravity, the most familiar of forces, still holds secrets that human understanding has not unraveled.
